analysis.one_liner: Requires at least two people, a certified engineer and conductor, on every freight train.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a Senate floor vote; it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The Safe Freight Act would have made it illegal to run a freight train with fewer than two crew members: one certified locomotive engineer and one certified train conductor. Every freight train, no matter how long or what technology it carries, would need a second pair of certified hands on board. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Freight train crews get a second certified worker on every train, which matters when something goes wrong mid-run and no one else is nearby for miles. Rail safety advocates argue two-person crews catch problems a lone operator can't, and communities along rail lines benefit from fewer runaway or mis-handled trains. Passengers and motorists crossing rail tracks also share in the safety gain.

how_it_helps.text: Bars any freight train or light locomotive moving freight from operating with fewer than two crew members, one certified as a locomotive operator and one as a train conductor.
The requirement would have taken effect 30 days after enactment, applying nationwide to all freight operations.

analysis.who_pays: Freight railroads, which have been moving toward one-person crews to cut labor costs, would have to keep paying for a second certified crew member on every train. Those costs could be passed along in shipping prices, and shortline railroads running low-traffic rural routes would feel the fixed-cost burden most.

drawbacks.text: The bill sets a flat two-person floor for every freight train regardless of route risk, train length, or onboard technology, so a two-car local pickup on a quiet branch line would need the same crew as a mile-long mainline train.
Railroads bear the added labor cost of a second certified employee on every train, a recurring expense that falls hardest on smaller, lower-revenue railroads.
The requirement starts just 30 days after enactment, leaving railroads little time to adjust staffing and training pipelines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety argument is straightforward: a second certified crew member is a backstop when a lone operator is incapacitated, misreads a signal, or faces an emergency miles from help. The cost is real but concentrated on the railroads' payroll, and the flat mandate ignores differences between mainline and light-duty operations. A better-drafted version might scale the requirement to risk, but as written the bill trades a modest, industry-borne cost for a uniform safety floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Heidi Heitkamp introduced the Safe Freight Act on January 30, 2018, joined by Sens. Baldwin, Brown, King, and Markey as original cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which was its last recorded action.
The bill ended the 115th Congress with no committee vote, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Freight railroads are better off: no federal two-person crew mandate was imposed, so railroads remain free to run one-person crews where allowed and keep the labor savings that the bill would have ended.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Freight railroads that avoided the crew mandate

for.name: Sen. Heidi Heitkamp
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Safe Freight Act and sent it to the Senate Commerce Committee.

for.name: Sens. Tammy Baldwin, Sherrod Brown, Angus King, and Ed Markey
for.what_they_did: Joined Heitkamp in introducing the bill at its introduction.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and never held a markup, hearing, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were Democrats or independents aligned with them; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-led Commerce Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would bar railroads from running one-person crews, requiring a second certified crew member on every freight train. That reverses the industry's move toward reduced crews and cuts into labor savings, which is why the industry's interest runs against the bill's safety purpose. [S2][S3]
A two-person minimum protects crew jobs and gives every train a second certified worker. The same backstop that protects workers protects the public from mishandled trains. [S2][S3]
